name: Ultimate attribution error
statement: Prejudiced observers explain a bad act by an outgroup member as the group's nature, and explain the same person's good act away as luck or an exception.
meaning: Pettigrew's proposal has two halves that point in opposite directions. A negative act by an outgroup member is read as disposition, in his wording often as genetically determined. A positive act by the same person is read as the exceptional case, as luck or special advantage, as high motivation and effort, or as a manipulable situational context. That second half is what separates the idea from the fundamental attribution error, which predicts a dispositional reading whatever the behaviour is. It also differs from in-group favouritism in what gets counted. Favouritism is measured in what people hand over, in money or cooperation; this is measured in the causes they name. Pettigrew put prejudice in the antecedent, writing that prejudiced people do this more than others, so the claim covers a subset of observers rather than everyone.

origin.note: The abstract outlines the cognitive contentions of Allport's The Nature of Prejudice, extends them with attribution theory, and proposes the error in two numbered predictions. It also says predictions are advanced about which of the four ways of discounting a positive outgroup act will be adopted and when the phenomenon will be magnified. Only that abstract was read, at Crossref and in the Wayback Machine's copy of the Sage article page, both on 21 September 2026. Sage itself answered every request with a Cloudflare bot challenge that day, under a browser user agent and a plain curl one alike, so the full text is unread and nothing here describes its argument beyond the abstract. Taylor and Jaggi's study in southern India came five years earlier, and the evidence section below rests on it.

evidence: Taylor and Jaggi asked Hindu participants to explain the behaviour of Hindu and Muslim actors performing socially desirable and socially undesirable acts, scoring internal against external causes. Their abstract reports internal attributions for ingroup actors doing desirable things and external attributions for ingroup actors doing undesirable things, with the converse for the same acts by Muslims. Sage answered every request for the article with a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026, so no means, cell sizes or test statistics from it appear on this page. Hewstone reviewed the literature eleven years after Pettigrew named the error. His abstract counts 19 studies across three paradigms, explanations for positive and negative outcomes, explanations for success and failure, and explanations for group differences, and says the ingroup-favouring tendency appears in most of them. It also says the evidence gives only limited support to Pettigrew's error, and that in any given study the bias is confined to particular dimensions. The three findings he calls strongest are more internal attribution for ingroup positive acts and less for ingroup negative acts, more attribution of outgroup failure to lack of ability alongside explaining outgroup success away as luck or effort or an easy task, and a preference for ingroup-serving accounts of group differences.

examples.text: A supporter who dislikes the visiting club calls a foul by their defender the sort of thing that club breeds, and a fine goal by the same defender a deflection. The bad act gets his nature and the good act gets his luck.

Staff who resent another team explain its missed deadline as how they operate and its delivered project as an easy brief. Both explanations are available at once, and which one gets used depends on whether the news is good.

A resident hostile to a group of new arrivals treats a noisy night as what they are like and a neighbour clearing the gutters as one decent one among them. The exception is granted precisely so the rule survives it.

replication.headline: Pettigrew's two predictions come apart under direct test. The positive-behaviour half survives, the negative-behaviour half does not, and one Delhi study was corrected to report no bias at all.
replication.detail: Khan and Liu tested both predictions with hypothetical scenarios among 148 Indians, 91 Hindu and 57 Muslim, and 145 Pakistanis, 107 Muslim and 38 Hindu. Their abstract reports that the first prediction, dispositional attribution of negative outgroup behaviour, received little support, and that the second, situational attribution of positive outgroup behaviour, received considerable but not total support. They call the overall result mixed and describe the pattern as ingroup favouring more than outgroup derogating. Khandelwal, Dhillon, Akalamkam and Papneja compared 321 Muslim adolescents, 239 male and 82 female, in Kashmir and in Delhi. The Kashmiri group made more ethnocentric attributions for ingroup positive behaviour, but not for the same behaviour by the outgroup. Neither did the two samples differ on socially undesirable behaviour by either group. Misra and Mishra ran 95 university students in Delhi, 51 from the General Caste category and 44 from the Scheduled Caste category, on success and failure scenarios scored for locus of causality, stability and controllability. The abstract as published reports no intergroup attribution bias in the General Caste group and ingroup derogation in the Scheduled Caste group. A correction printed in the same issue, on the pages directly after the article, rewrites that abstract to say both groups showed no intergroup attribution bias. It puts the pattern down to education, and asks that social desirability be probed in later work. Priedols, Dimdins, Gaina, Leja and Austers gave 222 Latvian students a policy initiative from a trusted or a distrusted party. Dispositional explanations moved as Pettigrew predicted, with success credited to a trusted party's benevolence, competence and integrity and failure blamed on a distrusted party's lack of them. Explanations by external circumstances showed no sign of the error. The largest effects in this area come from a design that is not Pettigrew's. Zell, Stockus and Bernstein asked American partisans how far Republican and Democratic policies had caused eight positive and 12 negative national outcomes, rated from 1 to 7. In Study 1, 244 MTurk workers in July 2016, the party by positive-credit by negative-blame interaction ran at F(1, 242) = 288.25, p < .001, partial eta squared .54. A summary bias index differed from zero at d = 1.21 among the 163 Democrats and d = 1.14 among the 81 Republicans. The preregistered Study 2, 249 registered voters in July 2020, gave F(1, 247) = 151.55, p < .001, partial eta squared .38, with the index at d = 0.85 among 135 Democrats and d = 0.73 among 114 Republicans. The two parties did not differ in either study, p = .134 and p = .288. What that measures is how much responsibility for an outcome each group is assigned, not whether one act gets an internal or an external cause.

study.cite: Khan, S. S., & Liu, J. H. (2008). Intergroup attributions and ethnocentrism in the Indian subcontinent: The ultimate attribution error revisited. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 39(1), 16-36.

limits: No effect size for the ultimate attribution error is quoted on this page, because none was obtained from a source that could be opened. Pettigrew's 1979 paper, Hewstone's 1990 review, Taylor and Jaggi's 1974 study and the Khan and Liu, Khandelwal, Misra and Priedols articles were all reached only as abstracts, and abstracts do not carry cell means or test statistics. The reasons differ, and this page names them rather than calling them all paywalls. Sage and Wiley each answered with a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026, to a browser user agent and to a plain curl one alike, which shut Pettigrew, Taylor and Jaggi, Khan and Liu, Hewstone and the openly licensed Priedols article. Elsevier answered the Allison and Messick page with a captcha the same day. The two Springer articles are genuine subscription content, and their article pages say so. That is why the structured fields above are empty and why the Zell figures, which come from a full text, sit in the prose with their design stated. No meta-analysis of intergroup causal attribution was located on 21 September 2026. The search covered Crossref by title and by bibliographic query, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, OpenAIRE, DOAJ, the Internet Archive and general web search, and turned up Hewstone's narrative review of 19 studies with no pooled estimate in its abstract. The Misra and Mishra article page shows the uncorrected abstract above a change history that carries the correction, so a reader who stops at the abstract gets ingroup derogation where the correction gives no bias. Every direct test read here used hypothetical scenarios or written vignettes rather than observed behaviour, and all of them are single samples from India, Pakistan, Kashmir or Latvia.
misreadings: The commonest reading treats this as the fundamental attribution error with a group swapped in for a person. It is not that. The fundamental attribution error predicts a dispositional reading of behaviour in general, while Pettigrew's second prediction is that a good act by an outgroup member gets a situational reading, which is the opposite direction. The half that keeps failing is the dispositional half, so the part of the idea that looks most like the fundamental attribution error is the part with the least support behind it. A second reading merges it with the group attribution error, which Allison and Messick named in 1985 and which this atlas holds at no. 300. Their abstract makes it a separate claim: the manipulation is the decision rule a group was bound by, and the inference runs from the group's decision to its members' attitudes. Prejudice and the valence of the act play no part in it. Group membership does, because two of their five experiments found a stronger inference from outgroup decisions than from ingroup ones. This page once carried group attribution bias as an alias, and that alias has been removed. A third reading collapses it into in-group favouritism. Favouritism is counted in allocations and cooperation between groups; this is a claim about the causes people give for one act, and the two can move apart. A fourth drops Pettigrew's condition. His abstract restricts both predictions to prejudiced people and says they will do this more than others, which makes prejudice a moderator rather than the effect being universal. The clause about attributing outgroup faults to genetics belongs to the original statement and is usually dropped in retelling. Zell and colleagues add a caution that applies to the whole family: a group-favouring attribution is a bias in the statistical sense, and bias in that sense does not by itself mean the attribution is wrong.

sources.text: Pettigrew, T. F. (1979). The ultimate attribution error: Extending Allport's cognitive analysis of prejudice. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 5(4), 461-476. Its abstract was read at Crossref on 21 September 2026, and again in the Wayback Machine's 2021 copy of the Sage article page. Sage itself answered the article and its PDF with a Cloudflare bot challenge that day, to a browser user agent and to a plain curl one alike. The full text was not reached. The volume index on the Internet Archive confirms the article opens at page 461.

Taylor, D. M., & Jaggi, V. (1974). Ethnocentrism and causal attribution in a South Indian context. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 5(2), 162-171. Described here from its abstract at Crossref, read on 21 September 2026, and no figure on this page comes from it. Sage answered the article with a Cloudflare bot challenge that day under two user agents, so the earlier note calling it paywalled named the wrong reason. The journal's volume index on the Internet Archive confirms the article opens at page 162.

Allison, S. T., & Messick, D. M. (1985). The group attribution error. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 21(6), 563-579. Cited for the separate phenomenon of that name. Its abstract, which names five experiments and the decision rules they manipulated, was read on 21 September 2026 in the Wayback Machine's 2012 copy of the Elsevier article page. Elsevier answered that page with a captcha the same day, and the full text was not obtained.

Hewstone, M. (1990). The 'ultimate attribution error'? A review of the literature on intergroup causal attribution. European Journal of Social Psychology, 20(4), 311-335. The count of 19 studies and the verdict of limited support are read from its abstract at Crossref, on 21 September 2026. Wiley answered the article and its PDF with a Cloudflare bot challenge that day under two user agents, and its text-mining endpoint refused the request, so the earlier note calling it paywalled named the wrong reason.

Khan, S. S., & Liu, J. H. (2008). Intergroup attributions and ethnocentrism in the Indian subcontinent: The ultimate attribution error revisited. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 39(1), 16-36. Described from its abstract at Crossref, read on 21 September 2026. Sage answered the article with a Cloudflare bot challenge that day, and no index listed an open copy.

Khandelwal, K., Dhillon, M., Akalamkam, K., & Papneja, D. (2014). The ultimate attribution error: Does it transcend conflict? The case of Muslim adolescents in Kashmir and Delhi. Psychological Studies, 59(4), 427-435. Described from the abstract on the publisher's article page, read on 21 September 2026 through rd.springer.com. The article is subscription content and the page says so; Crossref carries no abstract for it.

Misra, S., & Mishra, A. K. (2020). Is ultimate attribution error universal? Inter-group attribution for success and failure among university students in Delhi. Psychological Studies, 65(1), 64-73. The abstract on the publisher's page, read on 21 September 2026 through rd.springer.com, still reports ingroup derogation in the Scheduled Caste group, with the correction below carried underneath it as a change history. The article itself is subscription content.

Misra, S., & Mishra, A. K. (2020). Correction to: Is ultimate attribution error universal? Inter-group attribution for success and failure among university students in Delhi. Psychological Studies, 65(1), 74-75. Read in full on 21 September 2026, as a free PDF from rd.springer.com. It rewrites the abstract and the discussion to say both caste groups showed no inter-group attribution bias.

Open access under CC BY at the publisher, which answered the article, its PDF and its full-text XML with a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026, under two user agents. Described from its abstract at Crossref; DOAJ, OpenAIRE and OpenAlex list no location but Sage.

Zell, E., Stockus, C. A., & Bernstein, M. J. (2022). It's their fault: Partisan attribution bias and its association with voting intentions. Group Processes & Intergroup Relations, 25(4), 1139-1156. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from a hosted copy of the accepted online-first version, paginated 1 to 18 and dated 2021, whose figures match the record Crossref holds for the issue version. It is the only source here whose numbers were read off the paper.
